advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Make test_project_portability_docs.py derive the routing/template/prompt-path assertions from the real .rebar/ artifacts (or assert the doc matches them) so doc↔artifact drift is caught.
evidence: test_routing_example: `assert '"block_threshold": 0.9' in sub` (docs test line ~57) checks the doc's literal, not the config
Real config .rebar/criteria_routing.json:8 `"block_threshold": 0.9` is the authoritative value, read by the routing parser — the doc test does not compare the two

test_coaching_example asserts `_TEMPLATE in sub` where _TEMPLATE is a hardcoded copy of .rebar/plan_review_moves.json's template; the move JSON template could change and the doc-test copy would still match the (now-stale) doc
Sibling test_project_portability_criterion.py:59 already gates the REAL block_threshold==0.9, but nothing gates that the DOC agrees with it
advisory.finding: The new doc test asserts contract values as string literals present in docs/plan-review-gate.md but never cross-checks them against the real .rebar/ artifacts they claim to document, so doc/artifact drift passes silently (regression-blind). E.g. test_routing_example asserts `"block_threshold": 0.9` is in the doc prose; if .rebar/criteria_routing.json changes block_threshold to 0.8, the doc becomes wrong yet this test still passes because it only greps the doc's own hardcoded copy, not the source config.
scenarios: A future change edits block_threshold, the move template, or a routing facet in the .rebar/ artifact but forgets the doc — the doc silently drifts and every docs-test still passes
advisory.suggested_fix: In the routing/template/prompt-path assertions, load the real artifact (e.g. json.loads(.rebar/criteria_routing.json) and .rebar/plan_review_moves.json) and assert the doc contains the value taken FROM the artifact, so a change to the artifact that is not mirrored in the doc fails the test.

advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Either bind the calibration-threshold doc assertions to a committed source of truth, or drop test_calibration_example's exact-number checks as regression-blind prose assertions.
evidence: Doc test: `for threshold in ('recall: 1.0', 'false_accept: 0.0', 'agreement: 1.0', 'stability >= 0.6666666667', 'kappa >= 0.70'): assert threshold in sub` (test_project_portability_docs.py:127-134)

Real eval yaml has none of these tokens: `.rebar/evals/plan-review-project-portability.eval.yaml:14 gate: at_least(2)`, `:15 coverage_threshold: 1.0`, `:13 epochs: 3` — the doc's calibration numbers are prose with no artifact backing
The live-run thresholds are an [operator-attested] criterion per test_project_portability_eval.py:6-9, not a committed value, so the doc test can never be tied to a checkable source
advisory.finding: test_calibration_example asserts five threshold strings ('recall: 1.0', 'false_accept: 0.0', 'agreement: 1.0', 'stability >= 0.6666666667', 'kappa >= 0.70') exist in the doc, but none of these strings exist in the real eval spec .rebar/evals/plan-review-project-portability.eval.yaml (which uses gate: at_least(2), coverage_threshold: 1.0, epochs: 3). The assertion therefore cannot detect any regression in code or artifact behavior — it only verifies the author did not edit their own prose numbers, i.e. it is regression-blind.
scenarios: The live-calibration release thresholds are changed in practice/policy but the doc keeps stale numbers — the test passes; the numbers are unverifiable against any committed artifact
